answer.rationale:
The salient pressure (competitor entry pricing) pulls toward promotional_pricing, and memory_73 is the single most load-bearing claim for that path. It is also the most over-scoped record in the inheritance: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' plus a time-to-first-value gain plus generalization across both billing plans is a lot of conclusion for one archived test, and consolidated summaries tend to shed the caveats (segment, duration, discount depth, whether the lift was net of margin and churn). If that record turns out to be a short-window acquisition test on a narrow SMB cohort, discounting into a competitor's price war buys unqualified, price-shopping revenue and permanently resets willingness-to-pay — the opposite of the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective. So I spend verification there specifically because it is the option I am least willing to act on unverified.

Second pull is memory_86, because it and memory_31 may not be independent evidence. Both point at onboarding/signup for SMB activation, and memory_86 (day 52) reads like it could be a re-consolidation of memory_31 (day 12) rather than a separate result. Two memories agreeing feels like corroboration and is the exact place inherited memory inflates confidence. I want to know whether I have one finding or two before treating onboarding as well-supported.

Current intent is simplify_onboarding. The two observed declines are internal and upstream: onboarding completion (-4%) feeds activation (-6%), so repairing the funnel plausibly recovers both, and it strengthens the asset the competitor is attacking rather than conceding on price. activation_messaging (memory_91) treats the symptom downstream of the leak; referral_incentive (memory_57) requires an established base that a weakening activation funnel is not currently producing; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a real finding but addresses a segment that is not where this quarter's loss is occurring.

Explicit downstream risk: 'cutting required fields' is exactly the kind of change that lifts a proximate metric while degrading the thing we actually care about. Fewer fields means thinner qualification data, worse routing, and more low-intent signups — activation can rise while qualified revenue falls. So this runs with lead-quality, sales-acceptance, and 60–90 day retention/conversion as guardrails, not activation alone. If verification shows memory_86 and memory_31 are the same underlying test, or that its 'durable lift' was never measured past week one, I will hold scale down and reconsider activation_messaging, which has an independent record. If memory_73 comes back genuinely robust on margin and retention rather than raw acquisition, promotional_pricing moves back into contention as a defensive play.
